Unit 20 — Molecular-Dynamics Output as Data: Time Series, Convergence, Replicas and Free-Energy Statistics

A molecular-dynamics run produces a file with thousands of structures in it, and a student’s first instinct is to average something over them and compare it with the average of another run. That instinct produces most of the statistical errors in the simulation literature, because consecutive frames of a trajectory are not independent observations: a nanosecond of sampling can contain fewer than ten independent configurations. This unit takes six real simulations of the Trp-cage miniprotein — two temperatures, three replicas each — and treats their output exactly as what it is, a short, strongly autocorrelated multivariate time series. We measure how much information it actually contains, decide what to discard, compare the conditions in the two possible ways and watch them disagree by twenty-six orders of magnitude in the p-value, and then do the same careful accounting for fluctuations, projections, free-energy surfaces and cluster representatives.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad analiza la salida de una simulación de dinámica molecular como lo que es: una serie temporal corta y fuertemente autocorrelacionada. Con seis trayectorias reales de la miniproteína Trp-cage (dos temperaturas, tres réplicas cada una, 1 ns) se calculan la función de autocorrelación con acf(), el tiempo de autocorrelación integrado, la ineficiencia estadística y el tamaño de muestra efectivo; se promedia por bloques y se construye el gráfico de Flyvbjerg-Petersen; se detecta la equilibración con el promedio acumulado inverso y con el criterio de Chodera. El experimento central compara las dos condiciones de dos maneras: con las 3.000 tramas individuales (p del orden de 1e-26) y con las tres réplicas independientes (p = 0,69); la segunda es la honesta, porque la dispersión entre réplicas a la misma temperatura supera la diferencia entre temperaturas. Después se tratan las fluctuaciones por residuo como un problema de comparaciones múltiples con corrección BH, se reducen las coordenadas con prcomp y con un tICA implementado a mano, se lee un histograma bidimensional como superficie de energía libre con incertidumbre por bootstrap de bloques, y se agrupan las tramas para extraer estructuras representativas. La conclusión es siempre la misma: el número de réplicas, y no el número de tramas, determina lo que se puede afirmar.

Learning objectives

  • Treat molecular-dynamics observables (RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, distances, hydrogen bonds, energies) as correlated time series: autocorrelation function, integrated autocorrelation time, statistical inefficiency, effective sample size and block averaging.
  • Assess equilibration and convergence (reverse cumulative averaging, Chodera’s automated detection, replica agreement) and decide what to discard.
  • Compute uncertainties correctly across replicas and report them, applying the tests of Unit 8 to replica-level rather than frame-level data.
  • Reduce and cluster a conformational ensemble (PCA on Cartesian coordinates, tICA, k-means on the projection), read free-energy-like landscapes critically and attach sampling error to them.
  • Report energy decompositions of the MM/GBSA type with the statistics that hundreds of simultaneous per-residue comparisons demand.

How to read this unit

Read it linearly with the code running; every number quoted in the prose comes from a chunk of this same document. No simulation is run here and no trajectory file is parsed: the six runs arrive as frozen tables (md_trpcage_observables.csv, md_trpcage_rmsf.csv, md_trpcage_ca_coords.npz), so base R[30] plus data.table and ggplot2[26] suffice — in a fresh Google Colab R runtime run install.packages(c(“data.table”,“patchwork”)) once. The data folder also contains md_trpcage_strideA1.xtc and md_trpcage_protein.pdb, a 100-frame protein-only trajectory for students who want to repeat the measurements with MDTraj[8] or MDAnalysis[7] in Python; R has no equivalent trajectory parser in this environment, which is why the coordinates are read from the .npz archive instead (section 1 explains how). The unit uses the estimation vocabulary of Unit 7, the testing vocabulary of Unit 8 and the clustering of Unit 15. 

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})
set.seed(0)
PAL  <- c(blue = "#2b5d9b", orange = "#d2691e", green = "#3a7d44", purple = "#6a4c93")
RCOL <- c(A1 = "#2b5d9b", A2 = "#5b8bc9", A3 = "#8fb4e3",
          B1 = "#6a4c93", B2 = "#d2691e", B3 = "#a3421a")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
                panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
cat("R", paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
    "| data.table", as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
    "| ggplot2", as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")),
    "| patchwork", as.character(packageVersion("patchwork")), "\n")
## R 4.5.3 | data.table 1.18.6.1 | ggplot2 4.0.3 | patchwork 1.3.2

Everything below uses stats::acf, t.test, p.adjust, prcomp and kmeans from base R and the stats package: no simulation-analysis library is involved, because once the observables are tabulated the problem is ordinary time-series statistics.

1. What a production run leaves behind

Domain context

Molecular dynamics (MD) integrates Newton’s equations for every atom of a protein and its surrounding water, with forces given by an empirical energy function called a force field (here AMBER ff14SB[12] with TIP3P-FB water). A frame is the set of atomic coordinates saved at one instant — here every 2 picoseconds (ps), so a 1 nanosecond (ns) run leaves 500 frames. A replica is an independent repetition of the same simulation started with different random velocities; replicas differ because the dynamics are chaotic. The system here is Trp-cage, a designed 20-residue miniprotein[13] used as a test system since 2002 because it folds on the microsecond scale[14] — fast for a protein, still a thousand times longer than the runs analysed here. The quantities extracted per frame are: RMSD, the root-mean-square deviation of the C-alpha atoms from a reference structure after optimal superposition (a scalar measure of “how far the fold has moved”, in nm); Rg, the radius of gyration (compactness); the number of backbone hydrogen bonds; helix fraction, the proportion of residues assigned to a helix by the DSSP algorithm[15]; a side-chain distance defining the hydrophobic “cage”; and the thermostat and barostat readouts (instantaneous temperature, box volume, potential energy). RMSF is the root-mean-square fluctuation of one residue around its own average position — a per-residue measure of flexibility, not of displacement.

The six runs were produced with OpenMM 8[10][11] for this course: 4,810 atoms in a cubic box, 50 ps of NVT and 100 ps of NPT equilibration, then 1 ns of production sampling in the NPT ensemble, at 300 K (condition A) and 340 K (condition B), three seeds each. The protocol follows the current best-practice recommendations for foundations in molecular simulation[29]. The question they are meant to answer is the one a thesis student asks every week: does the protein behave differently at the higher temperature? Everything below is about answering that honestly with 1 ns of sampling — and about discovering how little 1 ns is.

Substitution — reading a NumPy archive from R

The superposed C-alpha coordinates are frozen in md_trpcage_ca_coords.npz, a NumPy archive. R has no reader for it, and no MDTraj/MDAnalysis equivalent is installed, so the first chunk below writes one: an .npz file is a ZIP container of .npy members, unzip() extracts them, and each .npy is a short ASCII header (dtype, shape, byte order) followed by the raw buffer, which readBin() reads directly. Twelve lines, no Python interpreter, and the arrays come out identical to numpy.load — the same reader is used in Unit 15. The alternative offered by the data folder, extracting coordinates from md_trpcage_protein.pdb plus the stride trajectory, would give only one of the six runs, so the archive is the right source. 

dp <- function(f) file.path("..", "data", f)      # knitr runs with cwd = this unit's folder
obs  <- fread(dp("md_trpcage_observables.csv"))
rmsf <- fread(dp("md_trpcage_rmsf.csv"))
RUNS <- c("A1", "A2", "A3", "B1", "B2", "B3"); DT <- 2      # ps between frames

read_npy <- function(path) {                       # minimal .npy reader
  con <- file(path, "rb"); on.exit(close(con)); readBin(con, "raw", 8)
  hlen  <- readBin(con, "integer", 1, size = 2, endian = "little")
  h     <- rawToChar(readBin(con, "raw", hlen))
  descr <- sub(".*'descr': *'([^']+)'.*", "\\1", h)
  dims  <- as.integer(Filter(nzchar, strsplit(
             gsub("[ )]", "", sub(".*'shape': *\\(([^)]*)\\).*", "\\1", h)), ",")[[1]]))
  x <- readBin(con, if (substring(descr, 2, 2) == "f") "double" else "integer",
               prod(dims), size = as.integer(substring(descr, 3)), endian = "little")
  if (length(dims) > 1) aperm(array(x, dim = rev(dims)), rev(seq_along(dims))) else x
}
nd <- file.path(tempdir(), "npz"); dir.create(nd, showWarnings = FALSE)
unzip(dp("md_trpcage_ca_coords.npz"), exdir = nd)
X <- do.call(rbind, lapply(RUNS, function(r) {     # 3000 frames x 60 coordinates (nm)
  a <- read_npy(file.path(nd, paste0(r, ".npy"))); t(apply(a, 1, function(m) as.vector(t(m)))) }))
time_ps <- read_npy(file.path(nd, "time_ps.npy"))
run_of  <- rep(RUNS, each = 500); time_of <- rep(time_ps, 6)
cat(sprintf("observables: %d x %d | rmsf: %d x %d | coordinates: %d frames x %d\n",
            nrow(obs), ncol(obs), nrow(rmsf), ncol(rmsf), nrow(X), ncol(X)))
## observables: 3000 x 11 | rmsf: 120 x 5 | coordinates: 3000 frames x 60
cat("columns:", paste(names(obs), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## columns: condition, replica, time_ps, rmsd_ca_nm, rg_nm, n_hbonds, helix_fraction, dist_W6_P12_nm, potential_energy_kJ_mol, temperature_K, box_volume_nm3
knitr::kable(obs[, .(frames = .N, rmsd_mean = mean(rmsd_ca_nm), rmsd_sd = sd(rmsd_ca_nm)),
                 by = .(condition, replica)][order(condition, replica)], digits = 4)
condition replica frames rmsd_mean rmsd_sd

A 2 500 0.1595 0.0110
A 3 500 0.2515 0.0212
B 1 500 0.1211 0.0138
B 2 500 0.1884 0.0333
B 3 500 0.1504 0.0337

Six runs of 500 frames, twenty residues, sixty coordinates per frame. The per-run means of the C-alpha RMSD already contain the whole story of the unit: at 300 K the three replicas sit at 0.110, 0.160 and 0.251 nm — a spread of 0.142 nm between repetitions of the same simulation.

obs[, run := paste0(condition, replica)]
p1 <- ggplot(obs, aes(time_ps, rmsd_ca_nm, colour = factor(replica))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ condition, nrow = 1,
             labeller = labeller(condition = c(A = "condition A - 300 K", B = "condition B - 340 K"))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange", "green")]), name = "replica") +
  labs(title = "The raw material: C-alpha RMSD against time",
       x = "time (ps)", y = "C-alpha RMSD (nm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p1)

Figure 1. C-alpha RMSD against time for the six runs. Within a condition the three replicas occupy clearly different bands — at 300 K the means are 0.110, 0.160 and 0.251 nm — and each trace wanders slowly, with excursions lasting tens to hundreds of picoseconds. Neither panel shows unfolding (RMSD stays below 0.35 nm); what they show is that each replica settled into its own region of conformational space and stayed there for the whole nanosecond.

Two features of Figure 1 decide the statistics of the whole unit. The traces are slow: a point is very similar to the point 20 ps before it, so the 500 frames of a run are not 500 observations. And the replicas disagree: the spread between replicas of the same condition (0.110 to 0.251 nm at 300 K) is larger than any difference the eye can find between the two conditions. Sections 2 and 5 turn those two observations into numbers.

2. Frames are not samples: autocorrelation and effective sample size

For a stationary time series \(x_1,\dots,x_N\) with mean \(\bar{x}\), the normalised autocorrelation function at lag \(k\) is

\[C(k) = \frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N-k}(x_t-\bar{x})(x_{t+k}-\bar{x})}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}(x_t-\bar{x})^2},\]

with \(C(0) = 1\). It answers “how much does a frame still tell me about a frame \(k\) steps later?”. Summing it gives the statistical inefficiency

\[g = 1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{k_{\max}} C(k),\]

the number of frames one must take to obtain one independent observation, and therefore the effective sample size \(N_{\text{eff}} = N/g\). The correct standard error of the mean is \(\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{eff}}}\), not \(\sigma/\sqrt{N}\) — an error of a factor \(\sqrt{g}\), which in this data is between 4 and 9. The integrated autocorrelation time in physical units is \(\tau_{\text{int}} = \Delta t\,(\tfrac{1}{2} + \sum_{k\ge 1}C(k))\), so that \(g = 2\tau_{\text{int}}/\Delta t\). The sum is truncated at the first zero crossing of \(C(k)\), because beyond it the estimator is pure noise[1][2].

Worked example: the autocorrelation of six numbers by hand

Take the series 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (mean 3.5; deviations -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, +0.5, +1.5, +2.5). The denominator is 6.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 + 6.25 = 17.5, so the variance term is 17.5/6 = 2.9167. For lag 1 the five products are (-2.5)(-1.5) = 3.75, (-1.5)(-0.5) = 0.75, (-0.5)(0.5) = -0.25, (0.5)(1.5) = 0.75 and (1.5)(2.5) = 3.75, summing to 8.75. Here the conventions part company: R’s acf() divides that sum by \(N = 6\), giving 8.75/6 = 1.4583 and \(C(1) = 1.4583/2.9167 = 0.500\); the “unbiased” convention divides by \(N - k = 5\), giving 1.75 and \(C(1) = 0.600\). The Python edition of this unit uses the second and therefore reports autocorrelation times about 10 % larger than the numbers below. Neither is wrong; the chunk prints both so that the difference is visible rather than mysterious. 

acf_vals <- function(x, nlags) as.numeric(acf(x, lag.max = nlags, plot = FALSE)$acf)
tau_g_neff <- function(x, dt = DT) {               # truncate the sum at the first zero crossing
  cc   <- acf_vals(x, length(x) %/% 2)
  zero <- if (any(cc <= 0)) which(cc <= 0)[1] - 1L else length(cc)
  s <- sum(cc[2:zero])
  c(tau = dt * (0.5 + s), g = 1 + 2 * s, n_eff = length(x) / (1 + 2 * s), zcross = (zero - 1) * dt)
}
toy <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6); dev <- toy - mean(toy)
cat(sprintf("by hand, 1/N convention   : var %.4f, lag-1 covariance %.4f, C(1) = %.3f\n",
            sum(dev^2) / 6, sum(dev[-6] * dev[-1]) / 6,
            (sum(dev[-6] * dev[-1]) / 6) / (sum(dev^2) / 6)))
## by hand, 1/N convention   : var 2.9167, lag-1 covariance 1.4583, C(1) = 0.500
cat(sprintf("by hand, 1/(N-k) convention: lag-1 covariance %.4f, C(1) = %.3f\n",
            sum(dev[-6] * dev[-1]) / 5, (sum(dev[-6] * dev[-1]) / 5) / (sum(dev^2) / 6)))
## by hand, 1/(N-k) convention: lag-1 covariance 1.7500, C(1) = 0.600
cat(sprintf("by stats::acf()            : C(1) = %.3f\n", acf_vals(toy, 2)[2]))
## by stats::acf()            : C(1) = 0.500

The hand calculation reproduces acf() exactly in its own convention, 0.500, and shows where the other convention’s 0.600 comes from. A monotone series is strongly autocorrelated, as it must be. The same estimator now goes to the real trajectories.

getcol <- function(r, col = "rmsd_ca_nm")
  obs[condition == substr(r, 1, 1) & replica == as.integer(substr(r, 2, 2))][[col]]
corr <- rbindlist(lapply(RUNS, function(r) {
  x <- getcol(r); t1 <- tau_g_neff(x); sd_ <- sd(x)
  data.table(run = r, rmsd_mean = mean(x), rmsd_sd = sd_, tau_rmsd_ps = t1[["tau"]],
             g = t1[["g"]], n_eff = t1[["n_eff"]], zcross_ps = t1[["zcross"]],
             tau_rg_ps = tau_g_neff(getcol(r, "rg_nm"))[["tau"]],
             se_naive = sd_ / sqrt(length(x)), se_correct = sd_ / sqrt(t1[["n_eff"]]),
             ratio = sqrt(t1[["g"]]))
}))
knitr::kable(corr, digits = 4)

Two things deserve attention. First the physics: the integrated autocorrelation time of the C-alpha RMSD is 17.7 to 80.2 ps depending on the replica, so the 500 frames of a 1 ns run contain between 6.2 and 28.3 independent observations. The naive standard error, 0.0005-0.0015 nm, under-estimates the real one by a factor \(\sqrt{g}\) of 4.2 to 9.0. (With \(\Delta t\) = 2 ps the columns \(\tau\) and \(g\) coincide numerically, because \(g = 2\tau/\Delta t\).) Any error bar on an MD average that was computed as \(\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{frames}}}\) is wrong by about that factor, and it is wrong in the dangerous direction.

Second the bookkeeping: the frozen summary file reports autocorrelation times about twice as large as ours (137.96 ps against 68.38 ps for run A1) and effective sample sizes correspondingly smaller, because it uses the convention \(\tau = \Delta t\,(1 + 2\sum_k C(k))\) — our \(g\) expressed in time units. Both appear in the literature and in simulation software[31]. The lesson is not that one is right — it is that “the autocorrelation time is 70 ps” is an incomplete statement: give the definition, the truncation rule and the frame interval, or give \(N_{\text{eff}}\) directly, which is unambiguous.

lagdf <- rbindlist(lapply(RUNS, function(r)
  data.table(run = r, condition = substr(r, 1, 1),
             lag = (0:125) * DT, C = acf_vals(getcol(r), 125))))
pa <- ggplot(lagdf, aes(lag, C, colour = run, linetype = condition)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, name = NULL) + scale_linetype(guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Autocorrelation of the RMSD", x = "lag (ps)", y = "C(k)") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.72), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
nedf <- rbind(data.table(run = corr$run, what = "independent samples", n = corr$n_eff),
              data.table(run = RUNS, what = "frames stored", n = 500))
pb <- ggplot(nedf, aes(run, n, fill = what)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_fill_manual(values = c(`frames stored` = "grey70",
                                                 `independent samples` = PAL[["blue"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Frames stored vs independent samples", x = NULL, y = "samples (log)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(pa | pb)

Figure 2. Left: the autocorrelation functions decay on very different time scales — runs A2 and B1 lose memory within about 80 ps, run B2 is still correlated at 176 ps. Right: the same information as a count. Every run stored 500 frames; between 6.2 and 28.3 of them are statistically independent. The ratio is the number that should govern every error bar in a simulation paper.

Exercise 1

Compute the integrated autocorrelation time of n_hbonds, helix_fraction and potential_energy_kJ_mol for run A1 with tau_g_neff(getcol(“A1”, “n_hbonds”)) and so on. Which observable decorrelates fastest, and why would you expect the potential energy of a 4,810-atom system to be the fastest of all? What does that imply about using the potential energy as evidence that a simulation is “converged”?

3. Block averaging and the Flyvbjerg-Petersen plot

The autocorrelation route needs a truncation rule. A route that needs none is block averaging: cut the series into \(M\) consecutive blocks of length \(b\), average within each block, and compute the standard error of those \(M\) block means. As \(b\) grows past the correlation time the block means become independent and the estimated standard error stops growing; the plateau value is the honest error bar. Plotting it against \(b\) is the Flyvbjerg-Petersen construction[3], and the shape of the curve is itself a diagnostic: if no plateau is reached before the blocks become too few to estimate anything, the run is too short for the quantity being measured.

block_se <- function(x, b) {                       # standard error from blocks of b frames
  m <- length(x) %/% b
  if (m < 2) return(NA_real_)
  sd(colMeans(matrix(x[1:(m * b)], nrow = b))) / sqrt(m)
}
bs  <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100)
blk <- as.data.frame(sapply(RUNS, function(r) sapply(bs, function(b) block_se(getcol(r), b))))
rownames(blk) <- paste0(bs * DT, " ps")
knitr::kable(blk, digits = 5, caption = "Standard error of the mean RMSD (nm) by block length")

  geom_hline(data = corr, aes(yintercept = se_correct, colour = run), linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Flyvbjerg-Petersen plot: no plateau means the run is too short",

  theme(legend.position = c(0.12, 0.72), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
print(p3)

Figure 3. Block-averaged standard error against block length for the six runs; dotted lines mark the autocorrelation-based estimate sigma/sqrt(N_eff) of section 2. The curves rise steadily and none flattens before 200 ps blocks, where only five blocks remain and the estimate itself becomes erratic — run A2 drops from 0.00173 to 0.00072 nm between the last two points, which is noise, not convergence. Where the two estimators can be compared they agree well (0.01343 against 0.01336 nm for run B2, 0.00537 against 0.00572 nm for A1) and both stand a factor of 4 to 9 above the naive sigma/sqrt(500) that most papers report.

A curve that has not plateaued is not a failure of the method; it is the method reporting that one nanosecond does not resolve the slowest motion contributing to this observable. The honest responses are to extend the simulation, to run more replicas, or to report an error bar derived from the replicas rather than from within a single run — which is what section 6 does, and what reviewers of simulation papers now expect[2][5].

4. Equilibration: deciding what to discard

The beginning of a production run is contaminated by relaxation from the starting structure. Two standard tools decide where that contamination ends. The reverse cumulative average plots the mean of the series computed from time \(t_0\) to the end, as a function of \(t_0\): while the system is still relaxing the curve drifts, and it flattens once the remaining data are stationary. Chodera’s automated criterion[4] formalises the trade-off — discarding data removes bias but costs samples — by choosing the \(t_0\) that maximises the effective sample size \(N_{\text{eff}}(t_0) = (N - t_0)/g(t_0)\) of the retained portion.

chodera_t0 <- function(x, dt = DT, step = 5) {
  n <- length(x); best <- c(0, -Inf)
  for (t0 in seq(0, as.integer(0.6 * n) - 1, by = step)) {
    seg <- x[(t0 + 1):n]
    if (length(seg) < 50) break
    ne <- length(seg) / tau_g_neff(seg)[["g"]]
    if (ne > best[2]) best <- c(t0, ne)
  }
  c(t0_ps = best[1] * dt, n_eff_after = best[2])
}
eq <- rbindlist(lapply(RUNS, function(r) {
  x <- getcol(r); b <- chodera_t0(x); kept <- x[(b[["t0_ps"]] / DT + 1):length(x)]
  data.table(run = r, t0_ps = b[["t0_ps"]], n_eff_after = b[["n_eff_after"]],
             mean_all = mean(x), mean_after = mean(kept), shift_nm = mean(kept) - mean(x))
}))
knitr::kable(eq, digits = 4)
run t0_ps n_eff_after mean_all mean_after shift_nm
A1 550 11.8000 0.1098 0.1198 0.010
A2 0 28.2162 0.1595 0.1595 0.000
A3 0 23.3593 0.2515 0.2515 0.000
B1 0 28.2536 0.1211 0.1211 0.000
B2 0 6.2351 0.1884 0.1884 0.000
B3 300 13.8433 0.1504 0.1374 -0.013 
cat(sprintf("mean |shift| caused by discarding: %.4f nm; largest %.4f nm (run %s)\n",
            mean(abs(eq$shift_nm)), max(abs(eq$shift_nm)), eq$run[which.max(abs(eq$shift_nm))]))
## mean |shift| caused by discarding: 0.0038 nm; largest 0.0130 nm (run B3)
t0s <- seq(0, 295, by = 5)
eqd <- rbindlist(lapply(RUNS, function(r) {
  x <- getcol(r)
  data.table(run = r, t0 = t0s * DT,
             mean_rest = sapply(t0s, function(t) mean(x[(t + 1):length(x)])),
             neff_rest = sapply(t0s, function(t) length(x) - t) /
                         sapply(t0s, function(t) tau_g_neff(x[(t + 1):length(x)])[["g"]]))
}))
pe1 <- ggplot(eqd, aes(t0, mean_rest, colour = run)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Reverse cumulative average", x = "discard everything before t0 (ps)",
       y = "mean RMSD of the rest (nm)") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.85, 0.55), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
pe2 <- ggplot(eqd, aes(t0, neff_rest, colour = run)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Chodera's criterion: maximise what is left", x = "t0 (ps)",
       y = "N_eff of the retained data")
print(pe1 | pe2)

Figure 4. Left: reverse cumulative averages. Four of the six runs are flat from the first frame — their 150 ps of equilibration was enough — while A1 drifts upwards and B3 downwards, by about 0.01 nm. Right: the effective sample size of the retained data. Its maximum is at t0 = 0 for four runs, at 550 ps for A1 and at 300 ps for B3, but the curves are noisy and shallow, which is the usual situation with so few independent samples: the criterion is choosing between nearly equivalent options.

The practical conclusion for this data set is that equilibration detection changes the means by at most 0.013 nm, an order of magnitude less than the between-replica spread of 0.142 nm. We therefore keep all 500 production frames of every run, and say so. That decision must be made and reported once, before the comparison between conditions — choosing a discard point per condition after looking at the comparison is a way of manufacturing a difference, and is the simulation version of the analytic flexibility that Unit 8 warns about.

5. The centrepiece: frame-level versus replica-level testing

Now the question the simulations were run to answer. Does the C-alpha RMSD differ between 300 K and 340 K? There are two ways to ask it with the same data.

The frame-level test pools all 1,500 frames of condition A against all 1,500 frames of condition B and runs Welch’s t-test[25]. The replica-level test first reduces each run to one number — its mean — and compares three numbers against three. The first treats frames as independent samples, which section 2 proved they are not: the effective number of independent configurations per condition is about 40 to 60, not 1,500, and even that counts correlated replicas separately. The second treats the replica as the experimental unit, which it is: replicas differ by their random seed exactly as biological replicates differ by their subject.

A <- obs[condition == "A", rmsd_ca_nm]; B <- obs[condition == "B", rmsd_ca_nm]
tf <- t.test(A, B)                                  # Welch by default in R
cat(sprintf("FRAME-LEVEL  : n = %d vs %d frames, means %.4f vs %.4f nm, Welch t = %.2f, p = %.3e\n",
            length(A), length(B), mean(A), mean(B), tf$statistic, tf$p.value))
## FRAME-LEVEL  : n = 1500 vs 1500 frames, means 0.1736 vs 0.1533 nm, Welch t = 10.81, p = 1.142e-26
mns <- dcast(obs[, .(m = mean(rmsd_ca_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)],
             condition ~ replica, value.var = "m")
a <- as.numeric(mns[condition == "A", -1]); b <- as.numeric(mns[condition == "B", -1])
tr <- t.test(a, b)
cat(sprintf("REPLICA-LEVEL: n = 3 vs 3 replica means %s vs %s\n",
            paste(round(a, 4), collapse = " "), paste(round(b, 4), collapse = " ")))
## REPLICA-LEVEL: n = 3 vs 3 replica means 0.1098 0.1595 0.2515 vs 0.1211 0.1884 0.1504
cat(sprintf("               means %.4f +/- %.4f vs %.4f +/- %.4f nm (SE over replicas), Welch t = %.3f, p = %.4f\n",
            mean(a), sd(a) / sqrt(3), mean(b), sd(b) / sqrt(3), tr$statistic, tr$p.value))
##                means 0.1736 +/- 0.0415 vs 0.1533 +/- 0.0195 nm (SE over replicas), Welch t = 0.443, p = 0.6895
cat(sprintf("\nratio of p-values: %.3g\n", tr$p.value / tf$p.value))
## 
## ratio of p-values: 6.04e+25
cat(sprintf("within-condition spread at 300 K: %.3f nm; difference between condition means: %.3f nm\n",
            max(a) - min(a), abs(mean(a) - mean(b))))
## within-condition spread at 300 K: 0.142 nm; difference between condition means: 0.020 nm

The frame-level test returns p = 1.1e-26 and the replica-level test returns p = 0.69 on the same numbers — a ratio of 6e25. Only one of them answers the scientific question. The frame-level test is not “more sensitive”; it is answering a different and uninteresting question — “do these 3,000 particular configurations come from the same distribution?” — with an n inflated fifty-fold by correlation. Its p-value would keep shrinking if the frames were saved every 0.2 ps instead of every 2 ps, without a single new configuration being sampled. That is the signature of a pseudo-replication error[5].

The honest answer is the second one: with three replicas per condition, a difference of 0.020 nm cannot be distinguished from the 0.142 nm spread between replicas at the same temperature. Trp-cage melts experimentally near 315 K but on the microsecond time scale[14], so one nanosecond at 340 K should not show unfolding — and does not.

ph <- ggplot(obs, aes(rmsd_ca_nm, fill = condition)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = PAL[["blue"]], B = PAL[["orange"]]),
                    labels = c("A (300 K)", "B (340 K)"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Frame level: p = %.0e", tf$p.value), x = "C-alpha RMSD (nm)", y = "frames") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.72, 0.8), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
repdf <- obs[, .(m = mean(rmsd_ca_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)]
pr <- ggplot(repdf, aes(condition, m, colour = condition)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = function(v) mean(v) - sd(v) / sqrt(3),
               fun.max = function(v) mean(v) + sd(v) / sqrt(3), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5, width = 0.25,
               geom = "errorbar") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = PAL[["blue"]], B = PAL[["orange"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("A (300 K)", "B (340 K)")) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Replica level: p = %.2f", tr$p.value), x = NULL, y = "mean RMSD per replica (nm)")
tempdf <- obs[, .(m = mean(temperature_K)), by = .(condition, replica)]
pt <- ggplot(tempdf, aes(condition, m, colour = condition)) + geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = PAL[["blue"]], B = PAL[["orange"]]), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "The control that does separate", x = NULL, y = "mean temperature (K)")
print(ph | pr | pt)

Figure 5. The same comparison seen three ways. Left: pooled frames, two broad overlapping histograms whose means differ by 0.020 nm — with 1,500 “samples” each, that difference is formally significant beyond any threshold. Centre: the three replica means per condition, with the standard error over replicas; the error bars overlap completely and the 300 K replicas straddle the 340 K ones. Right: the thermostat readout, where three replicas per condition suffice for an unmistakable separation (300.42 +/- 0.22 K against 340.24 +/- 0.07 K).

The right-hand panel is the control that makes the argument airtight. Replica-level testing is not insensitive: with exactly three replicas per condition it detects the temperature difference at p = 5.8e-06 and the box-volume difference (47.76 against 48.84 nm3) at p = 4.6e-07. It fails to detect a structural difference because there is no structural difference large enough to see in 1 ns, not because n = 3 is hopeless — the thermostat and the barostat[32] impose their targets identically in every replica, which is exactly the situation in which three replicas are plenty.

cols <- c("rmsd_ca_nm", "rg_nm", "n_hbonds", "helix_fraction", "dist_W6_P12_nm",
          "temperature_K", "box_volume_nm3")
summ <- rbindlist(lapply(cols, function(cl) {
  fa <- obs[condition == "A"][[cl]]; fb <- obs[condition == "B"][[cl]]
  m  <- obs[, .(mm = mean(.SD[[1]])), by = .(condition, replica), .SDcols = cl]
  ra <- m[condition == "A", mm]; rb <- m[condition == "B", mm]
  data.table(observable = cl, A = mean(ra), A_se = sd(ra) / sqrt(3), B = mean(rb), B_se = sd(rb) / sqrt(3),
             p_frame = t.test(fa, fb)$p.value, p_replica = t.test(ra, rb)$p.value)
}))
knitr::kable(summ, digits = 4)
observable A A_se B B_se p_frame p_replica
rmsd_ca_nm 0.1736 0.0415 0.1533 0.0195 0.000 0.6895
rg_nm 0.6910 0.0027 0.6903 0.0033 0.092 0.8758
n_hbonds 8.6993 0.5528 9.0533 0.2132 0.000 0.5985
helix_fraction 0.8822 0.0320 0.9174 0.0420 0.000 0.5437
dist_W6_P12_nm 0.5984 0.0078 0.5801 0.0152 0.000 0.3605
temperature_K 300.4248 0.2211 340.2414 0.0703 0.000 0.0000
box_volume_nm3 47.7625 0.0090 48.8373 0.0117 0.000 0.0000

Reading the table row by row is the habit to acquire. Four of the five structural observables have frame-level p-values between 2.4e-12 and 2.4e-30 and replica-level p-values between 0.36 and 0.88: every one of them would be reported as a “significant effect of temperature” by the frame-level analysis, and none survives the honest test. The fifth, the radius of gyration, is the instructive exception — it does not even reach significance at frame level (p = 0.092), because the two conditions really do have the same compactness to within the noise of 1,500 frames. The two instrument readouts behave in the opposite way: their frame-level p-values underflow to zero and their replica-level p-values are 5.8e-06 and 4.6e-07, because the thermostat and the barostat impose them identically in every replica. A results table of this shape, with both columns shown, is far more convincing to a reviewer than a single column of stars[2].

Exercise 2

Subsample each run by taking every fifth frame (obs[seq(1, .N, by = 5)] within each run, 100 frames per run instead of 500) and repeat both tests. The replica-level p-value should barely move; the frame-level one should rise by orders of magnitude. Explain in one sentence why the “significance” of the frame-level test is a property of the output-writing frequency rather than of the physics, and what that implies about trajectories saved every 0.1 ps.

6. Error bars from replicas

Once the replica is accepted as the unit of analysis, the recipe is short and is the one used in the group’s papers. Compute the observable per replica, average the replica values, and build the interval from the spread of those values with \(n =\) number of replicas:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i, \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad \text{CI}_{95\%} = \bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\,\mathrm{SE},\]

with \(t_{0.975,2} = 4.303\) for three replicas — more than twice the 1.96 of a large sample, which is what three replicas cost. The frames inside a replica are used only to compute \(x_i\); they never enter the error bar.

replica_ci <- function(v, conf = 0.95) {
  n <- length(v); se <- sd(v) / sqrt(n); h <- qt(0.5 + conf / 2, n - 1) * se
  c(mean = mean(v), se = se, lo = mean(v) - h, hi = mean(v) + h)
}
for (cd in c("A", "B")) {
  r <- replica_ci(if (cd == "A") a else b)
  cat(sprintf("condition %s: mean RMSD %.4f nm, SE %.4f, 95%% CI [%.4f, %.4f]  (t_0.975,2 = %.3f)\n",
              cd, r[["mean"]], r[["se"]], r[["lo"]], r[["hi"]], qt(0.975, 2)))
}
## condition A: mean RMSD 0.1736 nm, SE 0.0415, 95% CI [-0.0049, 0.3521]  (t_0.975,2 = 4.303)
## condition B: mean RMSD 0.1533 nm, SE 0.0195, 95% CI [0.0694, 0.2372]  (t_0.975,2 = 4.303)
d <- mean(b) - mean(a); pooled <- sqrt(var(a) / 3 + var(b) / 3)
cat(sprintf("\ndifference B - A = %+.4f nm, SE %.4f, 95%% CI [%+.4f, %+.4f]\n",
            d, pooled, d - 4.303 * pooled, d + 4.303 * pooled))
## 
## difference B - A = -0.0203 nm, SE 0.0458, 95% CI [-0.2176, +0.1770]
sd_rep <- sd(c(a - mean(a), b - mean(b)))
for (target in c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10))
  cat(sprintf("to detect a %.2f nm difference with 80 %% power one needs about %.0f replicas per condition\n",
              target, ceiling(2 * (2.8 * sd_rep / target)^2)))
## to detect a 0.02 nm difference with 80 % power one needs about 99 replicas per condition
## to detect a 0.05 nm difference with 80 % power one needs about 16 replicas per condition
## to detect a 0.10 nm difference with 80 % power one needs about 4 replicas per condition

The 95 % interval for the 300 K mean runs from -0.005 to 0.352 nm: with three replicas and this much spread, the data constrain the mean RMSD hardly at all (and the interval even reaches below zero, which an RMSD cannot be — a reminder that a normal-theory interval on n = 3 is a crude instrument). The interval for the difference, [-0.218, +0.177] nm, includes zero by a wide margin. The power calculation says what would be needed: with the observed between-replica standard deviation of 0.050 nm, detecting a 0.05 nm difference at 80 % power requires about sixteen replicas of this length, and a 0.02 nm difference about ninety-nine. That number — not the number of frames — is the one to put in a computing-time proposal, and it is why the field has moved from “one long run” to “many independent runs”[5][21].

7. Per-residue fluctuations: twenty tests at once

The RMSF table gives one number per residue per run: 20 residues × 6 runs. Comparing the conditions residue by residue is twenty simultaneous tests, and the multiple-comparison machinery of Unit 8 applies without modification (p.adjust(p, method = "BH") is base R’s Benjamini-Hochberg[24]). With three replicas per condition each individual test has almost no power, so the interesting output is not a list of significant residues but the honest statement that the data do not support one.

rf <- rmsf[, {
  ra <- rmsf_nm[condition == "A"]; rb <- rmsf_nm[condition == "B"]
  .(resname = resname[1], A = mean(ra), B = mean(rb), diff = mean(rb) - mean(ra),
    p = t.test(ra, rb)$p.value)
}, by = residue]
rf[, q_BH := p.adjust(p, method = "BH")]
cat(sprintf("mean C-alpha RMSF: A %.4f nm, B %.4f nm  (+%.0f %% at the higher temperature)\n",
            mean(rf$A), mean(rf$B), 100 * (mean(rf$B) / mean(rf$A) - 1)))
## mean C-alpha RMSF: A 0.0594 nm, B 0.0743 nm  (+25 % at the higher temperature)
cat(sprintf("residues with raw p < 0.05: %d of 20 | with BH q < 0.05: %d | smallest raw p = %.3f, smallest q = %.3f\n",
            sum(rf$p < 0.05), sum(rf$q_BH < 0.05), min(rf$p), min(rf$q_BH)))
## residues with raw p < 0.05: 0 of 20 | with BH q < 0.05: 0 | smallest raw p = 0.060, smallest q = 0.619
gm <- rmsf[, .(m = mean(rmsf_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)]
cat(sprintf("one global test on the mean RMSF per replica instead of twenty: p = %.3f\n",
            t.test(gm[condition == "A", m], gm[condition == "B", m])$p.value))
## one global test on the mean RMSF per replica instead of twenty: p = 0.276
knitr::kable(head(rf[order(p)], 5), digits = 4)
residue resname A B diff p q_BH
15 GLY 0.0645 0.0879 0.0233 0.0600 0.6191
1 ASN 0.0986 0.1230 0.0244 0.0719 0.6191
20 SER 0.1125 0.1643 0.0518 0.1287 0.6191
18 PRO 0.0534 0.0769 0.0236 0.1771 0.6191
3 TYR 0.0442 0.0664 0.0222 0.1850 0.6191 
rbar <- rmsf[, .(m = mean(rmsf_nm), se = sd(rmsf_nm) / sqrt(3)), by = .(condition, residue)]
rbar <- merge(rbar, rf[, .(residue, resname)], by = "residue")
rbar[, lab := factor(sprintf("%s%d", resname, residue),
                     levels = sprintf("%s%d", rf$resname[order(rf$residue)], sort(rf$residue)))]
pf1 <- ggplot(rbar, aes(lab, m, fill = condition)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.75) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = m - se, ymax = m + se), position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = PAL[["blue"]], B = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Per-residue fluctuation, mean +/- SE over 3 replicas", x = NULL, y = "C-alpha RMSF (nm)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, size = 5.5, vjust = 0.5), legend.position = "bottom")
pf2 <- ggplot(rf, aes(diff, -log10(p))) + geom_point(size = 1.6, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = min(rf$diff), y = -log10(0.05) + 0.06, label = "p = 0.05", hjust = 0, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = head(rf[order(p)], 3), aes(label = sprintf("%s%d", resname, residue)),
            nudge_y = 0.05, size = 2.4) +
  labs(title = "Twenty tests, none surviving correction",
       x = "RMSF difference B - A (nm)", y = "-log10 p (raw)")
print(pf1 | pf2)

Figure 6. Left: per-residue C-alpha RMSF with the standard error over the three replicas. The familiar shape is there — the termini and the Gly-Gly-Pro loop fluctuate most — and the 340 K bars are on average 25 % higher (0.0743 against 0.0594 nm). Right: the same comparison as a volcano-style plot. Not one of the twenty residues reaches raw p < 0.05 (the smallest is p = 0.060 at Gly15, and the largest difference, +0.052 nm at the C-terminal Ser20, has p = 0.129) and the smallest BH-adjusted q-value is 0.619.

This is a textbook demonstration of two statistical facts at once. A systematic 25 % increase that is visible in every replica is still not significant when each residue is tested with three values per group, because the between-replica variance is large and a t-test on n = 3 needs a very large effect. And testing twenty residues multiplies the chance of a false positive, so the Benjamini-Hochberg correction pushes the adjusted values further up. The right report is therefore: “mean C-alpha RMSF increased from 0.059 to 0.074 nm at 340 K; with three replicas no individual residue reached significance after FDR correction”. Even the single global test on the replica mean RMSF — one test instead of twenty, and therefore more power — returns p = 0.276, so the increase is not established by this data set either way. Fewer tests, more power, and an answer to the question that was actually asked.

8. Projections: principal components and tICA

A frame of this system is 20 C-alpha positions, that is a point in 60-dimensional space; all six runs together are a 3,000 × 60 matrix, already superposed on the same reference. Principal component analysis finds the orthogonal directions of largest positional variance — in the simulation literature this is called essential dynamics[16] — and projecting the frames onto the first two gives the picture everybody draws. The caveat that must accompany that picture was published almost as early as the method itself: with short trajectories the leading components are dominated by the slowest motion that happened to occur, and projections of different runs can look like different states purely from lack of sampling[17][18].

Time-lagged independent component analysis (tICA) changes the objective: instead of maximising variance it maximises autocorrelation at a chosen lag time, so its leading components are the slowest collective coordinates rather than the widest[6]. It is the standard first step of Markov-state modelling[22][23]. No R package implements it here, so the next chunk writes it: a generalised eigenvalue problem in fifteen lines of matrix algebra, which is also the best way to understand what it does.

Y   <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)$x        # 3000 x 60 projection
evr <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)$sdev^2
evr <- evr / sum(evr)
cat("PCA explained variance ratio:", round(evr[1:5], 3),
    sprintf("| first three together: %.3f\n", sum(evr[1:3])))
## PCA explained variance ratio: 0.465 0.213 0.07 0.042 0.038 | first three together: 0.748
for (r in RUNS) {
  m <- run_of == r
  cat(sprintf("   %s  PC1 %+.3f (sd %.3f)   PC2 %+.3f\n", r, mean(Y[m, 1]), sd(Y[m, 1]), mean(Y[m, 2])))
}
##    A1  PC1 -0.330 (sd 0.097)   PC2 -0.045
##    A2  PC1 -0.037 (sd 0.093)   PC2 +0.269
##    A3  PC1 +0.595 (sd 0.096)   PC2 -0.055
##    B1  PC1 -0.262 (sd 0.111)   PC2 -0.050
##    B2  PC1 +0.197 (sd 0.222)   PC2 +0.177
##    B3  PC1 -0.162 (sd 0.130)   PC2 -0.296
tica <- function(Z, groups, lag) {        # whiten with C(0), diagonalise the symmetrised C(lag)
  p <- ncol(Z); C0 <- matrix(0, p, p); Ct <- matrix(0, p, p); n <- 0
  for (g in unique(groups)) {
    W  <- scale(Z[groups == g, ], scale = FALSE)
    aa <- W[1:(nrow(W) - lag), ]; bb <- W[(lag + 1):nrow(W), ]
    C0 <- C0 + crossprod(aa) + crossprod(bb)
    Ct <- Ct + crossprod(aa, bb) + crossprod(bb, aa)
    n  <- n + 2 * nrow(aa)
  }
  C0 <- C0 / n; Ct <- Ct / n
  e  <- eigen(C0, symmetric = TRUE); w <- pmax(e$values, 1e-12)
  Wh <- e$vectors %*% diag(w^-0.5) %*% t(e$vectors)      # whitening matrix
  M  <- Wh %*% Ct %*% Wh
  ee <- eigen((M + t(M)) / 2, symmetric = TRUE); o <- order(-ee$values)
  list(ev = ee$values[o], proj = scale(Z, scale = FALSE) %*% (Wh %*% ee$vectors[, o]))
}
LAG <- 20                                                # frames = 40 ps
tc  <- tica(Y[, 1:10], run_of, LAG)
its <- -LAG * DT / log(pmin(pmax(tc$ev[1:4], 1e-9), 0.999))
cat(sprintf("tICA at lag %d ps: eigenvalues %s\n", LAG * DT, paste(round(tc$ev[1:4], 3), collapse = " ")))
## tICA at lag 40 ps: eigenvalues 0.798 0.612 0.61 0.489
cat("implied timescales (ps):", round(its, 1), " <- compare with the 1000 ps length of each run\n")
## implied timescales (ps): 177.1 81.4 80.8 55.8  <- compare with the 1000 ps length of each run
pdf1 <- data.table(run = run_of, PC1 = Y[, 1], PC2 = Y[, 2], t1 = tc$proj[, 1], t2 = tc$proj[, 2])
pp1 <- ggplot(pdf1, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = run)) + geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2))) +
  labs(title = "PCA: colour = run, not condition",
       x = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f %%)", 100 * evr[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f %%)", 100 * evr[2])) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.88, 0.72), legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
        legend.key.height = unit(7, "pt"))
pp2 <- ggplot(data.table(k = 1:10, cum = cumsum(evr[1:10])), aes(k, cum)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL[["blue"]]) + geom_point(colour = PAL[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  labs(title = "Two components carry 68 %", x = "number of components", y = "cumulative variance explained")
pp3 <- ggplot(pdf1, aes(t1, t2, colour = run)) + geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RCOL, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "tICA at a 40 ps lag", x = "tIC1", y = "tIC2")
print(pp1 | pp2 | pp3)

Figure 7. Left: the first two principal components explain 46 % and 21 % of the positional variance, and the six runs occupy six nearly disjoint islands — run A3 sits at PC1 = +0.60 while A1 is at -0.33, although both are at 300 K. Centre: the cumulative variance curve; three components reach 75 %. Right: the tICA projection at a 40 ps lag, which separates the runs just as sharply because the slowest motion in this data set is precisely the drift of each replica into its own basin.

The left panel is the figure a student is most tempted to over-interpret. It does not show “the free-energy landscape of Trp-cage at two temperatures”; it shows that each 1 ns run visited one region and that the regions differ between runs of the same condition as much as between conditions. The tICA timescales say the same thing numerically: the slowest implied timescale at a 40 ps lag is 177 ps, a fifth of the trajectory length, and estimates of implied timescales become unreliable once they approach the simulation length. A converged ensemble would show the six clouds overlapping, which is the practical convergence test to apply before any landscape is published[18][21].

9. A two-dimensional histogram is not a free-energy surface until it has error bars

Given an equilibrium ensemble, the probability \(P(x,y)\) of being in a bin of a projection is related to a free energy by \(F = -k_BT \ln P\) (up to an additive constant), with \(k_BT = 2.49\) kJ/mol at 300 K. Two conditions must hold for that equation to mean anything: the sampling must be at equilibrium, and each bin must contain enough independent frames for \(P\) to be estimated. Section 2 showed we have at most 28 independent frames per run, so the second condition is already in trouble. The remedy is to estimate the uncertainty of \(F\) the same way the mean was estimated — by resampling whole blocks of frames with the bootstrap[33], which preserves the correlation inside a block.

kT <- 0.0083145 * 300                                     # kJ/mol at 300 K
xe <- seq(min(Y[, 1]), max(Y[, 1]), length.out = 31)
ye <- seq(min(Y[, 2]), max(Y[, 2]), length.out = 31)
hist2 <- function(x, y) {
  ix <- pmin(pmax(findInterval(x, xe, rightmost.closed = TRUE), 1), 30)
  iy <- pmin(pmax(findInterval(y, ye, rightmost.closed = TRUE), 1), 30)
  matrix(as.numeric(table(factor(ix, 1:30), factor(iy, 1:30))), 30, 30)
}
H <- hist2(Y[, 1], Y[, 2]); P <- H / sum(H)
Fs <- -kT * log(ifelse(P > 0, P, NA)); Fs <- Fs - min(Fs, na.rm = TRUE)
blocks <- unlist(lapply(RUNS, function(r) split(which(run_of == r), rep(1:10, each = 50))),
                 recursive = FALSE)                       # 100 ps blocks
set.seed(0)
boot <- replicate(100, {
  pick <- unlist(blocks[sample(length(blocks), length(blocks), TRUE)])
  p <- hist2(Y[pick, 1], Y[pick, 2]); p <- p / sum(p)
  f <- -kT * log(ifelse(p > 0, p, NA)); f - min(f, na.rm = TRUE)
})
sdF  <- apply(boot, 1:2, function(v) sd(v, na.rm = TRUE))
well <- is.finite(Fs) & H >= 20
cat(sprintf("occupied bins: %d of 900 | bins with >= 20 frames: %d\n", sum(is.finite(Fs)), sum(well)))
## occupied bins: 366 of 900 | bins with >= 20 frames: 40
cat(sprintf("apparent depth using ALL occupied bins: %.1f kJ/mol (this is the number not to quote)\n",
            max(Fs, na.rm = TRUE)))
## apparent depth using ALL occupied bins: 9.9 kJ/mol (this is the number not to quote)
cat(sprintf("free-energy range over well-populated bins: %.2f kJ/mol\n", max(Fs[well]) - min(Fs[well])))
## free-energy range over well-populated bins: 2.48 kJ/mol
cat(sprintf("bootstrap-over-blocks uncertainty there: median %.2f kJ/mol, maximum %.2f kJ/mol\n",
            median(sdF[well], na.rm = TRUE), max(sdF[well], na.rm = TRUE)))
## bootstrap-over-blocks uncertainty there: median 1.06 kJ/mol, maximum 1.61 kJ/mol
cat(sprintf("ratio of the apparent range to its own uncertainty: %.1f\n",
            (max(Fs[well]) - min(Fs[well])) / median(sdF[well], na.rm = TRUE)))
## ratio of the apparent range to its own uncertainty: 2.3
xc <- (xe[-31] + xe[-1]) / 2; yc <- (ye[-31] + ye[-1]) / 2
fdt <- data.table(x = rep(xc, 30), y = rep(yc, each = 30),
                  F = as.vector(Fs), sd = as.vector(ifelse(well, sdF, NA)))
pf_a <- ggplot(fdt[is.finite(F)], aes(x, y, fill = F)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1, name = "kJ/mol") +
  labs(title = "-kT ln P over the PCA projection", x = "PC1", y = "PC2")
pf_b <- ggplot(fdt[is.finite(sd)], aes(x, y, fill = sd)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "kJ/mol") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(fdt$x), ylim = range(fdt$y)) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap-over-blocks uncertainty", x = "PC1", y = "PC2")
print(pf_a | pf_b)

Figure 8. Left: the two-dimensional histogram of the pooled 3,000 frames converted to -kT ln P over its 366 occupied bins. It looks like a landscape with several minima separated by barriers of up to 9.9 kJ/mol. Right: the standard deviation of the same quantity over 100 bootstrap resamples of 100 ps blocks, restricted to the 40 bins with at least 20 frames. The uncertainty there is about 1.1 kJ/mol over a usable range of 2.5 kJ/mol — the apparent structure is roughly two standard deviations deep — and the sparsely populated regions that carry the deepest “barriers” are absent from the right panel altogether, because single blocks decide whether they are occupied at all.

Three rules follow, and they apply equally to the free-energy surfaces the group publishes for larger systems. Mask bins below a stated occupancy instead of letting one frame create a minimum. Attach an uncertainty obtained by resampling blocks (or, better, by comparing independent replicas) rather than frames. And never convert a histogram to a free energy when the ensemble is not equilibrium sampling — after a biased or steered simulation the transformation requires reweighting, which is the business of enhanced-sampling methods[28].

10. Clustering frames and extracting representative structures

Clustering a trajectory serves a practical purpose: to replace 3,000 frames by a handful of structures that can be drawn in a figure, docked, or submitted as supplementary coordinates. The algorithm is the k-means of Unit 15 applied to the projection, and the representative of a cluster is the frame closest to its centre. The diagnostic that matters is not the silhouette score but the cross-tabulation of clusters against runs.

set.seed(0)
km <- kmeans(Y[, 1:5], centers = 4, nstart = 10)
ct <- table(run = run_of, cluster = km$cluster)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame.matrix(ct), caption = "Frames of each run per cluster")
Frames of each run per cluster
1 2 3 4
A1 0 3 497 0
A2 1 0 0 499
A3 500 0 0 0
B1 0 15 471 14
B2 187 0 0 313
B3 0 329 163 8 
for (k in 1:4) {
  m   <- which(km$cluster == k)
  dk  <- sqrt(rowSums((Y[m, 1:5] - matrix(km$centers[k, ], length(m), 5, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  rep_i <- m[which.min(dk)]
  cat(sprintf("cluster %d: %4d frames (%4.1f %%) | representative: run %s at %4d ps | RMSD there %.3f nm | runs with > 20 frames: %s\n",
              k, length(m), 100 * length(m) / nrow(Y), run_of[rep_i], time_of[rep_i],
              obs$rmsd_ca_nm[rep_i], paste(rownames(ct)[ct[, k] > 20], collapse = ", ")))
}
## cluster 1:  688 frames (22.9 %) | representative: run B2 at  736 ps | RMSD there 0.240 nm | runs with > 20 frames: A3, B2
## cluster 2:  347 frames (11.6 %) | representative: run B3 at  566 ps | RMSD there 0.142 nm | runs with > 20 frames: B3
## cluster 3: 1131 frames (37.7 %) | representative: run B1 at  760 ps | RMSD there 0.106 nm | runs with > 20 frames: A1, B1, B3
## cluster 4:  834 frames (27.8 %) | representative: run A2 at  104 ps | RMSD there 0.155 nm | runs with > 20 frames: A2, B2
ctd <- as.data.table(ct)
pcl1 <- ggplot(ctd, aes(factor(cluster), run, fill = N)) + geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = N), size = 2.6, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL[["purple"]], high = PAL[["blue"]], name = "frames") +
  labs(title = "Frames of each run per cluster", x = "cluster", y = NULL)
pcl2 <- ggplot(data.table(PC1 = Y[, 1], PC2 = Y[, 2], cl = factor(km$cluster)),
               aes(PC1, PC2, colour = cl)) + geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.35) +
  annotate("point", x = km$centers[, 1], y = km$centers[, 2], shape = 4, size = 2.4, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL), name = "cluster") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2))) +
  labs(title = "k-means (k = 4) on the first five PCs")
print(pcl1 | pcl2)

Figure 9. Left: how the frames of each run distribute over the four clusters. Run A3 is entirely in cluster 1, A2 almost entirely in cluster 4 (499/500), A1 almost entirely in cluster 3 (497/500) and B1 94 % in that same cluster; only B2 (187/313) and B3 (329/163) are genuinely split between two clusters. Right: the same partition in the PC1-PC2 plane. The clusters are compact and well separated — and they are the replicas.

A clustering that recovers the replica labels is reporting that the ensemble is not converged, not that the protein has four metastable states. Published as “the four dominant conformational states of Trp-cage”, it would be an artefact; published as “each 1 ns replica remains within one basin, and the basins differ between replicas”, it is a correct and useful statement about sampling. The representative structures are still perfectly usable as illustrations — cluster 3, sampled by A1, B1 and part of B3, is the most native-like with RMSD 0.106 nm at its representative frame — provided the caption says they are representatives of what was sampled rather than of equilibrium populations. A cluster population is only an equilibrium probability if the ensemble is converged, which here it is not.

11. Reporting an energy decomposition

Binding-free-energy estimates of the MM/PBSA and MM/GBSA family[9] are computed frame by frame and are usually accompanied by a per-residue decomposition. Everything in this unit applies to them, and more sharply, because the numbers are large and their differences are small. Three requirements are not optional. First, the error bar on a mean interaction energy must come from independent blocks or replicas, never from \(\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\text{frames}}}\): energies decorrelate fast but the conformations that generate them do not. Second, a per-residue table of 200 residues compared between two systems is 200 simultaneous tests and needs the false-discovery-rate control of section 7; the usual presentation, a bar chart of the ten largest contributions, is a selection effect by construction. Third, the absolute value of an MM/GBSA energy is not a binding free energy — comparisons within one system and one protocol are defensible, comparisons across protocols are not. A reviewer who sees “ligand A: -45.2 +/- 0.3 kcal/mol, ligand B: -43.8 +/- 0.3 kcal/mol, therefore A binds better” is reading a standard error computed over correlated frames of a single trajectory, and the correct response is to ask for the replicas.

pe <- getcol("A1", "potential_energy_kJ_mol")
t_pe <- tau_g_neff(pe)
cat(sprintf("run A1 potential energy: mean %.0f kJ/mol, sd %.0f\n", mean(pe), sd(pe)))
## run A1 potential energy: mean -79538 kJ/mol, sd 272
cat(sprintf("  tau_int = %.1f ps, N_eff = %.1f of 500 frames\n", t_pe[["tau"]], t_pe[["n_eff"]]))
##   tau_int = 1.8 ps, N_eff = 271.4 of 500 frames
cat(sprintf("  naive SE = %.1f kJ/mol | autocorrelation-corrected SE = %.1f | 100 ps block SE = %.1f\n",
            sd(pe) / sqrt(500), sd(pe) / sqrt(t_pe[["n_eff"]]), block_se(pe, 50)))
##   naive SE = 12.2 kJ/mol | autocorrelation-corrected SE = 16.5 | 100 ps block SE = 12.9
cat(sprintf("  replica-level SE over the three 300 K runs = %.1f kJ/mol\n",
            sd(sapply(c("A1", "A2", "A3"), function(r) mean(getcol(r, "potential_energy_kJ_mol")))) / sqrt(3)))
##   replica-level SE over the three 300 K runs = 1.5 kJ/mol

The potential energy of the whole system is the instructive counterexample, and it is worth reading carefully. It decorrelates in 1.8 ps, so 271 of the 500 frames of run A1 are effectively independent and the three within-run error bars agree within a factor of 1.4 (12.2 kJ/mol naive, 16.5 autocorrelation-corrected, 12.9 from 100 ps blocks). The replica-level standard error is smaller, 1.5 kJ/mol, because the total potential energy of 4,810 atoms is dominated by the water box, which the three runs equilibrated to the same value (-79,538, -79,534 and -79,539 kJ/mol). So “use replicas” is not a ritual that always inflates error bars: it is an instruction to match the error bar to the slowest motion the quantity depends on. A total energy depends on fast solvent degrees of freedom and converges quickly; an RMSD, an RMSF or an MM/GBSA interaction energy depends on the conformation of a few residues, whose relaxation is the slow motion this unit has been measuring all along — and those are the quantities whose published error bars are routinely a factor of five to ten too small.

12. Summary

Six real nanosecond trajectories of a 20-residue protein were analysed here with no simulation software, only the frozen tables they produced and base R. The accounting came first: the integrated autocorrelation time of the C-alpha RMSD is 17.7 to 80.2 ps depending on the replica, so each run of 500 stored frames contains between 6.2 and 28.3 independent configurations and the naive standard error is too small by a factor of 4.2 to 9.0. Block averaging agreed with the autocorrelation estimate where both could be computed (0.01343 against 0.01336 nm for B2), and the Flyvbjerg-Petersen curves never reached a plateau — the data telling us that 1 ns does not resolve the slowest contributing motion. Equilibration detection by reverse cumulative averaging and by Chodera’s effective-sample-size criterion moved the means by at most 0.013 nm, so all frames were kept, and that decision was taken before any comparison.

Then the central experiment. Pooling frames, the two temperatures differ in C-alpha RMSD with p = 1.1e-26; comparing the three replica means per condition, the same data give p = 0.69, with condition means of 0.174 +/- 0.041 and 0.153 +/- 0.019 nm. The 300 K replicas alone span 0.110 to 0.251 nm, a spread seven times the difference between the conditions. Three more structural observables behave identically — frame-level p-values from 2.4e-12 to 2.4e-30, replica-level p-values from 0.36 to 0.60 — while the thermostat and barostat readouts are significant by both routes (300.42 +/- 0.22 K against 340.24 +/- 0.07 K, p = 5.8e-06; 47.76 against 48.84 nm3, p = 4.6e-07), proving that n = 3 is not the obstacle. A power calculation on the between-replica standard deviation of 0.050 nm says that detecting a 0.05 nm difference would need about sixteen replicas, and a 0.02 nm difference about ninety-nine.

The same discipline reshaped every downstream analysis. Per-residue RMSF rose by 25 % on average at 340 K (0.059 to 0.074 nm) yet no residue of twenty reached raw p < 0.05, let alone an FDR-corrected one, and the single global test on the replica means returns p = 0.276. PCA put the six runs in six nearly disjoint islands (PC1 means from -0.33 for A1 to +0.60 for A3, both at 300 K) and tICA at a 40 ps lag separated them further, with a slowest implied timescale of 177 ps — a fifth of the run length. The -kT ln P surface built from the pooled frames showed apparent minima of 9.9 kJ/mol, but a bootstrap over 100 ps blocks gave an uncertainty near 1.1 kJ/mol over a defensible range of only 2.5 kJ/mol across the 40 bins holding at least 20 frames. k-means on the projection returned four clean clusters that are, almost exactly, the six replicas. The potential energy was the counterexample that sharpens the rule: it decorrelates in 1.8 ps and its replica-level error bar (1.5 kJ/mol) is smaller than its within-run one, because a total energy is dominated by fast solvent motion rather than by the slow conformational relaxation that governs every structural observable.

None of this means the simulations were useless: it means that what 1 ns × 6 supports is a description of what was sampled, error bars built from replicas, and an honest statement of what could not be resolved. The three habits to carry away are to quote \(N_{\text{eff}}\) whenever an MD average is reported, to make the replica the unit of analysis in every test, and to put the uncertainty of a landscape or an energy decomposition next to the landscape itself[1][2][27]. Microsecond studies of this same protein[19][20] exist precisely because the honest analysis of a nanosecond says so little.

Bridge

Within this course: the confidence intervals and the bootstrap come from Unit 7, the tests, power and FDR control from Unit 8, PCA from Unit 13, and k-means and the same .npz reader from Unit 15. The previous unit, Unit 19, treated the output of a screening pipeline with the same attitude: correlated samples, honest error bars, and a benchmark interrogated rather than believed. The Python edition of this unit, which reads the archive with numpy.load and uses scikit-learn for the projection, is here. In the sister courses: how these trajectories are produced, from structure preparation to thermostats, is BGM324 unit 5 (molecular dynamics), with the structural background in BGM324 unit 2; the free-energy and docking context is in BGM324 unit 4, and the machine-learning background in BGM411 (R edition).

13. Self-assessment

  1. A paper reports “RMSD = 0.21 +/- 0.01 nm (mean +/- SEM over 5,000 frames)”. What is wrong, and what would you ask for?

The standard error was computed as sigma/sqrt(N_frames), which assumes independent frames. With an autocorrelation time of tens of picoseconds the effective sample size is one or two orders of magnitude smaller, so the quoted uncertainty is too small by sqrt(g). Ask for the integrated autocorrelation time or N_eff, a block-averaging plot, or — best — the per-replica means and an error bar built from them.

  1. Why does saving frames more often make a frame-level t-test “more significant” without adding information?

Because the test’s n is the number of saved frames, while the information content is set by the number of independent configurations, N_eff = N/g. Halving the output interval doubles N and leaves N_eff unchanged, so the p-value falls while nothing has been learnt. This is pseudo-replication.

  1. State the difference between the statistical inefficiency g and the integrated autocorrelation time, and why two analyses of the same run can report autocorrelation times differing by a factor of two.

g = 1 + 2 sum_k C(k) is dimensionless and equals the number of frames per independent sample; tau_int = dt(1/2 + sum_k C(k)) has units of time and satisfies g = 2 tau_int/dt. Some software reports dt(1 + 2 sum C(k)) = g dt instead, which is exactly twice tau_int — the factor of two seen between our table and the frozen summary file. A second, smaller source of disagreement is the normalisation of the autocorrelation estimator itself: R’s acf() divides by N, the “unbiased” convention by N - k. Always give the definition or report N_eff.

  1. Your Flyvbjerg-Petersen curve rises monotonically and never plateaus. What are your options?

The run is shorter than the slowest motion affecting the observable. Extend it, add independent replicas and build the error bar from the replica means, or restrict the claim to an observable that does decorrelate within the run. Reporting the last computable block value as “the” error bar understates the uncertainty.

  1. Four of six runs need no equilibration discard and two need 300-550 ps. Should you discard the same amount from every run?

Applying a common, pre-registered discard (for instance the first 100 ps of every run) is defensible and simple; applying a per-run automated criterion is also defensible. What is not defensible is choosing per-run discards after seeing how they affect the comparison between conditions. Decide the rule first, report it, and show that the conclusion does not depend on it.

  1. With three replicas per condition the temperature difference is detected at p = 6e-06 but the RMSD difference is not detected at all. What does that prove?

That n = 3 is not inherently powerless: when the effect is large relative to the between-replica spread, three replicas suffice. The failure to detect an RMSD difference is therefore evidence that the structural effect is small compared with replica-to-replica variation at 1 ns, not evidence that the test is too weak to be used.

  1. How many replicas would you request to detect a 0.05 nm difference in mean RMSD, and what did that estimate assume?

About sixteen per condition, from the observed between-replica standard deviation of 0.050 nm, 80 % power and a two-sided 5 % level. It assumes that the replica means are approximately normal and that the spread observed with three replicas is a reasonable estimate — itself very uncertain with two degrees of freedom, so treat the number as an order of magnitude.

  1. A PCA plot shows two separated clouds for two trajectories of the same system. Name two innocent explanations before “two conformational states”.

Insufficient sampling — each run relaxed into a different basin and never crossed back, which is exactly what Figure 7 shows — and the projection itself, since the leading components are chosen to maximise the variance that happens to be present, so any slow drift becomes PC1. A convergence check is whether independent replicas overlap in the projection.

  1. What must accompany a -kT ln P landscape for it to be interpretable?

The occupancy threshold used to mask sparse bins, an uncertainty estimated by resampling blocks or by comparing replicas, a statement that the sampling is unbiased equilibrium sampling (or the reweighting scheme if it is not), and the temperature used in kT. Here the uncertainty was about 1.1 kJ/mol against a usable depth of 2.5 kJ/mol, while the unmasked figure suggested 9.9 kJ/mol.

  1. k-means on your trajectory projection returns clusters that coincide with the replicas. What do you report?

That the ensemble is not converged: each replica remained in its own basin. The representative structures may still be shown as illustrations of what was sampled, but cluster populations must not be presented as equilibrium probabilities, and the number of clusters must not be presented as a number of metastable states.

  1. A collaborator sends a per-residue MM/GBSA decomposition for two ligands and asks which residues differ. What do you do first?

Count the tests. A 200-residue table is 200 comparisons; control the false-discovery rate with p.adjust(…, method = “BH”), use replica-level or block-level error bars rather than per-frame ones, and refuse to interpret the ten largest bars as a finding, since selecting them after looking is a selection effect. Report effect sizes with intervals, not stars.

  1. Section 11 found a replica-level error bar on the potential energy that was smaller than the within-run one. Does that contradict the rest of the unit?

No. The replica-level error bar is the right one in both cases; it is simply small here, because the total potential energy is dominated by solvent degrees of freedom that decorrelate in picoseconds and reach the same mean in every run. The rule is to match the error bar to the slowest motion the quantity depends on, and for conformational observables that motion is slower than one nanosecond.

Glossary

Frame
One set of coordinates saved from a trajectory; here one every 2 ps, 500 per run.
Replica
An independent repetition of a simulation with a different random seed; the experimental unit for statistics.
RMSD
Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions from a reference after optimal superposition; a measure of how far a structure has moved.
RMSF
Root-mean-square fluctuation of a residue around its own mean position; a measure of local flexibility.
Autocorrelation function C(k)
Normalised correlation between a series and itself k steps later; C(0) = 1. Computed here with stats::acf.
Integrated autocorrelation time
tau_int = dt(1/2 + sum_k C(k)); the time scale over which the series loses memory.
Statistical inefficiency g
1 + 2 sum_k C(k) = 2 tau_int/dt; the number of frames needed per independent sample.
Effective sample size
N_eff = N/g; the number of independent observations a correlated series is worth.
Block averaging
Estimating the standard error from the means of consecutive blocks; the estimate plateaus once blocks exceed the correlation time.
Flyvbjerg-Petersen plot
Block-averaged standard error against block length; absence of a plateau means the run is too short.
Equilibration detection
Choosing the portion of a run to discard, e.g. by reverse cumulative averaging or by maximising the retained effective sample size.
Pseudo-replication
Treating correlated observations (frames) as independent experimental units, inflating n and deflating p-values.
Essential dynamics / PCA
Principal component analysis of atomic coordinates; the leading components are the directions of largest positional variance.
tICA
Time-lagged independent component analysis: the linear projection maximising autocorrelation at a chosen lag, hence the slowest collective coordinates.
Implied timescale
-lag/ln(eigenvalue); an estimate of a relaxation time, trustworthy only when much shorter than the trajectory.
Free-energy surface
-kT ln P over a projection; meaningful only for equilibrium sampling, with masked sparse bins and a stated uncertainty.
MM/GBSA
End-point method estimating interaction energies frame by frame from a molecular-mechanics energy plus an implicit-solvent term; relative use within one protocol only.

Textbooks

  • Leach AR. Molecular Modelling: Principles and Applications. 2nd ed. Pearson; 2001. - Chapters 6-7 for the mechanics behind the trajectories analysed here.
  • Tuckerman ME. Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Molecular Simulation. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press; 2023. - Ensembles, thermostats and the meaning of a free-energy surface.
  • Wasserman L. All of Statistics. Springer; 2004. - Chapter 8 for the bootstrap used on blocks here.
  • Shumway RH, Stoffer DS. Time Series Analysis and Its Applications: With R Examples. 4th ed. Springer; 2017. - The autocorrelation machinery of section 2, from the time-series side.

Online resources

  • LiveCoMS best-practices collection for molecular simulation: livecomsjournal.org.
  • pymbar, the reference implementation of equilibration detection and statistical inefficiency: pymbar.readthedocs.io.
  • OpenMM user guide, the engine that produced these trajectories: docs.openmm.org.
  • CRAN Task View “Time Series Analysis”, for the estimators of section 2: cran.r-project.org/view=TimeSeries.
  • bio3d, an R package for structural bioinformatics and PCA of trajectories (not installed in this course environment): thegrantlab.org/bio3d.
